title: The Flood
summary: Genesis 6-9 narrates divine judgment on pervasive violence, Noah's preservation through a flood, the post-flood human vocation, and God's covenant sign of the bow.
historical_context: The narrative belongs to Genesis's primeval history. Its event chronology and literary formation are debated, so the entry distinguishes the narrated world from the dates of surviving Mesopotamian flood witnesses.
ancient_near_east_context: Mesopotamian flood traditions such as Atrahasis and Gilgamesh Tablet XI offer specific shared motifs and substantial differences. Comparison establishes an ancient literary environment but does not by itself prove direct borrowing or identify archaeological flood deposits with Genesis.
hebraic_worldview: Genesis attributes judgment, preservation, blessing, and covenant to one God and grounds post-flood human accountability in the divine image.
literary_context: Genesis 6-9 moves from human corruption and violence through the ark and receding waters to sacrifice, blessing given again, and covenant. Repeated dates, measurements, divine speeches, and reversals organize the account.
covenantal_significance: In Genesis 8:20-9:17, God promises the stability of the earth's cycles, reaffirms human fruitfulness and accountability, and gives the bow as the sign of the covenant with Noah, his descendants, and living creatures.
canonical_role: The flood closes the first cycle of primeval violence and judgment, leads into the covenant with Noah, and becomes a later biblical analogy for judgment, preservation, and covenant faithfulness.

related_objects.notes: Noah's family, preservation, sacrifice, and covenant frame the narrative.
The evidence cluster preserves chronology and limits for Gilgamesh and other Mesopotamian comparisons.

scripture_references.notes: Corruption, divine judgment, Noah, and the ark instructions.
Entry into the ark and the flood.
Later prophetic appeal to the waters of Noah and God's covenant faithfulness.

interpretive_notes.note: Read the complete movement from violence and judgment to post-flood blessing and covenant rather than reducing the narrative to a search for a flood deposit.
Shared flood motifs warrant literary comparison, but a surviving Mesopotamian tablet is neither an eyewitness record of Genesis nor proof of direct dependence.
